task: Iteration 5 of the great-dirac-w0ytk7 autonomous loop. Iterations 1-4 narrowed compiler_ms (build_completion_forest's timer) to 94.95-97.76% of the exposure12 champion's hero/button/callout smoke-suite wall time, but none split what happens *inside* a single compiler_ms call. This session directly measures, for one isolated hero-record decode replay, whether a single compiler_ms call is dominated by the Node/TypeScript compiler-bridge round trip (the working hypothesis carried into this iteration from the prior doc chain) or by pure-Python compiler work.

method.summary: Two bounded, CPU-only measurements against a tiny scratch TwoTowerModel (d_model=32, 1 layer) built directly from smoke_hero_01's gold OpenUI source, bypassing full eval-harness/checkpoint construction to stay well inside the 3-minute wall.

measurement_1_call_split.what: Token-by-token replay of smoke_hero_01's gold source through the real decode call path (build_completion_forest(..., remaining_tokens=...), the exact function twotower.py's compiler-tree per-position loop calls), capped at 12 calls / 90s wall so the run always terminates and emits partial data. _generated_ast_is_complete (the one call site per build_completion_forest invocation that invokes the Node bridge, via lang_core.parse) was unwrapped from its lru_cache and timed directly per call.

measurement_2_cprofile_one_call.what: cProfile of a single representative slow call (position idx=2 of the same replay, ~10.5s in measurement 1's 12-call sample, ~33.5s standalone in a fresh profiled run -- run-to-run variance itself noted, see caveats).

hot_path.role: Proves each candidate completion path in the forest can actually reach EOS within the remaining decode budget (docstring: 'prove each action reaches EOS'). Recursion is lru_cache(maxsize=64)-bounded and capped at nodes_left=16, but the lru_cache is defined *inside* _tail_from's closure, so it is fresh (empty) on every one of the 32 top-level (primitive) invocations -- no cache sharing across sibling candidate-path searches within the same build_completion_forest call.

Each _tail recursion node builds a fresh OpenUIIncrementalEngine() (no state/engine reuse passed down -- _tail_from calls _build_openui_completion_forest without a state argument), forcing a full re-lex + re-parse from scratch, then probes reachable next-terminals via Lark's LALR accepts(), which internally copies the parser stack (731012 feed_token calls, 548517 parser-state copy() calls) to test candidates non-destructively.

Re-lexes each candidate prefix from scratch per recursion node (no incremental engine reuse across _tail nodes); this is the layer iteration 1's Lark lexer/scanner cache (PR #1173) targeted -- correctly identified as inside the hot path, but a small minority of it, which is consistent with iteration 1's REJECT finding that caching it alone did not move wall-clock.

hot_path.function: compiler_draft.py:1139 _generated_ast_is_complete -> lang_core.parse -> lang_core._invoke_repl (Node bridge, persistent REPL)
hot_path.role: The Node-bridge round trip, invoked once per _build_openui_completion_forest call (including every recursive _tail node, 264 times total within this single 33.5s outer call). Confirms measurement 1's aggregate finding at the deep-recursion level too: the bridge itself is cheap and is not amortization-limited -- the persistent-REPL path (lang_core.py's _invoke_repl, already the default since before this iteration) means each of the 264 calls pays essentially zero subprocess-spawn cost (median well under 2ms).

falsifiable_question: Is a single compiler_ms call dominated by Node process/bridge round-trip overhead (IPC, subprocess spawn/reuse, serialization) or by actual pure-Python compiler work, and does the persistent-REPL bridge (already the default via lang_core.py's _invoke_repl) mean the Node-bridge round trip is negligible now that the Lark lexer cache (PR #1173, iteration 1) has landed?
result: ANSWERED -- pure-Python compiler work dominates overwhelmingly; the Node bridge is negligible (well under 1% at every granularity measured)
decision: REJECT the carried-over working hypothesis that the Node/TypeScript compiler-bridge round trip is the dominant or even a meaningfully explanatory cost inside compiler_ms. Across the 12-call aggregate replay, the bridge accounts for 0.02% of total time (13.98ms of 58416ms); inside one deep-recursion profiled call, the bridge accounts for 0.8% (0.267s of 33.5s) even though it is invoked 264 times in that single outer call. The true dominant cost is pack.py's _tail/_tail_from recursive reachability-proof search: for one build_completion_forest call, it drives 32270 fresh engine syncs (each re-lexing and re-parsing from scratch, since no engine/state is threaded through the recursion) and 32270 calls into Lark's InteractiveParser.accepts(), which is itself expensive per-call because it copies the interactive-parser state to probe candidates non-destructively.
interpretation: This corrects, rather than confirms, the framing carried into this iteration from the prior doc chain's next-steps section (decode-compiler-tree-timeout-telemetry-restore-20260728.md: 'Consider whether the Node-bridge round trip itself ... is amortizable -- a persistent bridge process instead of one-shot subprocess.run per call would be a genuinely new architectural direction'). That persistent-REPL bridge already exists (lang_core.py's _invoke_repl, _ensure_repl, module-global _REPL_PROC, default path since before this iteration) and is not the bottleneck at all -- the framing that motivated this iteration's own task brief ('compiler_ms ... is now unambiguously the dominant, unexplained cost ... the Node/TypeScript compiler-bridge round trip per decode step') does not survive contact with per-call instrumentation. It also refines iteration 1's REJECT verdict on the Lark lexer/scanner cache (PR #1173): that cache targets exactly the _lex_tokens/_lex layer this session measured at ~17.5% of one call's cost -- real, but a minority contributor next to the _tail_from reachability search's own state-reconstruction-per-node cost (48%+ in Lark's accepts() alone), which explains why caching the lexer in isolation did not move the wall-clock outcome. The single biggest architectural fact this session surfaces: _tail_from's recursion (pack.py:392-419) calls _build_openui_completion_forest directly, per candidate node, without threading through the caller's incremental engine/state -- so every reachability-proof node pays a full relex+reparse instead of extending shared incremental parser state, and the lru_cache meant to bound repeated (current, room) pairs is scoped inside the closure and does not persist across the ~32 sibling top-level searches within one call.
scope_note: No claim about the exposure12 champion's quality or promotion status. No decode_outcome, latency, or deadline-semantics change (no source code was edited this session -- pure instrumentation of a standalone tiny scratch model, not the eval harness). No claim that fixing _tail_from's engine reuse would close the 30s wall entirely -- only that it is now the measured, evidenced hot path, displacing the Node-bridge hypothesis this iteration was framed around.
non_goals: No code fix attempted or landed -- the _tail_from reachability-search architecture (threading engine/state through recursive candidate-path proof search, and/or sharing its lru_cache across sibling top-level searches) is a genuine architectural change, explicitly out of scope for a bounded 3-minute-wall iteration per this iteration's own instructions.
No change to decode_timeout_seconds, deadline semantics, or outcome classification.
No GPU or real-scale training run -- tiny scratch model (d_model=32, 1 layer), CPU only.
No claim that the Node bridge is irrelevant everywhere -- only that it is not the compiler_ms bottleneck for this suite's decode-time completion-forest construction path.
next_steps: If a future iteration wants to reduce compiler_ms, the evidenced next target is pack.py's _tail_from/_tail closure (lines 392-419): thread the caller's already-synced OpenUIIncrementalEngine/state through each recursive candidate-path node instead of constructing a fresh engine per node, and/or hoist the lru_cache above the per-call closure boundary so sibling top-level candidate searches within one build_completion_forest invocation can share proof results. Both are real architectural changes (out of scope this session) that would need their own bounded, falsifiable before/after measurement.

Consider whether _tail_from's nodes_left=16 budget and Lark's accepts()-based reachability probe could be replaced with the same lexer/parser-state-cache strategy PR #1173 already applied elsewhere, now correctly scoped to the _tail recursion's fresh-engine-per-node pattern rather than the top-level call.

Re-run measurement 1's call-split protocol against the real exposure12 checkpoint (not this session's tiny scratch model) if a future session wants a production-scale confirmation that the same 0.02%/99.98% bridge/rest split holds at full model width.
caveats: measurement_2's standalone call (33.5s) is larger than measurement_1's same-position call inside the 12-call batch (~10.5s at idx=2) -- run-to-run variance on a shared CPU sandbox is expected and does not change the qualitative conclusion (bridge negligible, pack.py _tail dominant) since the bridge's absolute cost (0.267s) and share (0.8%) were measured directly in the same profiled run, not inferred from the other run.

This session used a tiny from-scratch TwoTowerModel (d_model=32, 1 layer, seed 0) built directly from smoke_hero_01's gold text, not the exposure12 champion checkpoint -- chosen to stay inside the 3-minute wall (loading/evaluating through the full eval harness with the champion checkpoint was iteration 4's approach and itself burns most of the 30s decode-timeout budget per record). The qualitative hot-path finding (recursive reachability search >> Node bridge) is a property of the compiler_draft.py/pack.py/engine.py code path itself, not of this particular tiny model's weights, but absolute per-call milliseconds are not directly comparable to iteration 4's champion-checkpoint numbers.

candidates_returned=27 for the profiled call is consistent with, not identical to, the counts iteration 4 saw for whole-record runs (17/86/31 forwards for hero/button/callout) -- this session profiles one isolated position, not a full record.
